title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbook, and Benchmarking Suite
author: Maya Patel
content:
Purpose

This document consolidates the serving runtime team’s canonical reference for runtime architecture, kernel scheduling principles, the profiling and benchmarking playbook, release notes summary for recent runtime releases, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended for engineers owning the runtime, SREs, and platform teams integrating with the runtime.

Scope

- Runtime architecture overview (components, ownership, SLOs).
- Kernel and scheduler design and tuning guidance.
- Profiling playbook (how to profile tail latency, memory, and KV-cache behavior).
- Benchmarking suite and standardized workload recipes.
- Release notes template + recent highlights.
- Known issues and workarounds.
- Runbooks and team wiki links for oncall and upgrades.

1) High-level runtime architecture

Overview
- The serving runtime is composed of three logical layers: Ingress & Router, Inference Engine (GPU worker processes), and Observability & Control Plane.
- Primary services: routerd (request routing and policy), inferd (inference worker), cache-proxy (KV prefix caching), profile-agent (local metrics aggregation), and runtime-control (rollouts & model pinning).

Component responsibilities
- routerd: request validation, routing by policy (latency-first, cost-first, region), per-route quotas, and canary routing. SLA owner: Runtime Platform.
- inferd: single-process GPU executor that manages model kernels, KV cache, per-request batching, and token streaming. Executor owner: Serving Runtime Team.
- cache-proxy: local NVMe-backed cache for KV/prefix caching with eviction and admission policy. Owner: Serving Runtime Team.
- profile-agent: collects p95/p99 latency histograms, per-kernel utilization counters, and memory watermarks. Owner: Observability.

SLOs and targets (global defaults)
- p95 token latency: <= 75ms for short responses (<= 256 tokens).
- p99 token latency: <= 250ms for short responses.
- tail request latency (99.9th): <= 1.5s.
- per-node GPU utilization target (steady-state): 40–85% depending on workload mix.

Ownership and contact points
- Serving runtime: @serving-runtime (team alias), primary owner: Maya Patel.
- Observability & Metrics: @eng-platform (for histogram and tracing QA).
- Capacity & Fleet: @eng-sre for GPU node lifecycle.

2) Kernel selection and scheduling principles

Design goals
- Minimize per-token latency while maximizing throughput and efficient GPU utilization.
- Provide predictable latency SLOs using fast-path kernels for short sequences and progressive kernels for long sequences.

Kernel selection rules (high level)
1. Short sequences (<= 128 tokens remaining): prefer fused attention kernels (fast path) -> lower latency.
2. Medium sequences (129–1024): use tiled attention kernels tuned per-arch.
3. Long sequences (>1024): use streaming-friendly kernels with KV-remote optimizations and reduced precision where acceptable.

Scheduler behavior and tuning knobs
- Continuous batching: inferd collects requests for up to 2ms or until a configured batch size threshold. Config: BATCH_WAIT_MS (default 2), BATCH_MAX_TOKENS.
- Priority preemption: small low-latency batches are prioritized over large throughput batches when latency policy is active. Toggle: LATENCY_FIRST=true|false.
- Kernel warm pools: Keep N pre-loaded kernels per model variant per GPU (config KERNEL_POOL_SIZE, default 2).
- Memory reservation: We reserve 8% of GPU memory for transient allocations by default; set via GPU_RESERVED_MEM_MB.

Common tuning recipes
- Low-latency workloads: set BATCH_WAIT_MS=1, enable LATENCY_FIRST, ensure KERNEL_POOL_SIZE>=2.
- Throughput-heavy workloads: increase BATCH_WAIT_MS to 4–8ms, increase BATCH_MAX_TOKENS, enable mixed-precision kernels.

3) Profiling playbook (step-by-step)

When to run profiling
- After significant kernel changes, new model variants, or changes to batching logic.
- When p99/p999 latency increases or GPU OOMs appear in production.

Quick checklist
1. Reproduce workload: capture representative request traces for 30–60 minutes using trace-sampler.
2. Run end-to-end synthetic replay: ./tools/replay_workload --trace traces/serving-2026-01-12.json --concurrency N --seed=42.
3. Run per-node microprofiling: ./tools/node_profiler --target inferd://node-123 --duration 120s --metrics kernel,mem,sm_activity.
4. Collect GPU/kernel flamegraphs: ./tools/flamegen --pid <inferd-pid> --out flame-<node>.svg.
5. Analyze histograms: use /internal/metrics/ui -> compare p50/p95/p99 before/after changes.

Key artifacts to collect
- request traces (sampled), kernel-level timelines, GPU SM utilization heatmaps, per-kernel latency distributions, memory high-water marks, and KV cache hit/miss rates.

Success criteria
- No >15% regression in p95 latency for short sequences; p99 within negotiated bounds.
- Memory watermarks do not exceed configured headroom (GPU_RESERVED_MEM_MB).
- KV cache hit ratio within expected +/-5% of baseline.

4) Benchmarking suite and standard workloads

Overview
- The benchmarking suite (bench/) lives in the monorepo and contains workload recipes, recorder, and reporting tools. Bench artifacts are versioned and stored in s3://redwood-bench-results.

Standard workloads
- small-chat: short instruction->response (avg 32 tokens). Target: measure token p95/p99, cold-start time.
- llm-chat-med: mixed length chat (avg 256 tokens). Target: throughput and memory usage.
- long-context: 8k–32k token workloads to test KV checkpointing and streaming kernels.
- embeddings-bulk: batch embeddings throughput for 16k vectors.

Running benchmarks
1. Checkout monorepo and set BENCH_BUCKET and AWS creds.
2. Ensure test cluster with matching instance types (g5.12xlarge equivalent) and pristine nodes.
3. Run: ./bench/run_bench --workload small-chat --replicates 5 --report s3://redwood-bench-results/runtime/2026-02-01/
4. Compare against baseline: ./bench/compare --baseline s3://redwood-bench-results/runtime/baseline-2026-01-01 --target s3://...

Reporting and acceptance
- Bench runs must include raw traces, per-kernel latency distributions, and a summary CSV.
- Changes to scheduling or kernels require bench regressions to be <=5% for p95 in short-chat workload before promoting to production.

5) Release notes (runtime) — recent highlights

Release: runtime v3.8.0 (2026-02-10)
- Improved fused attention kernel selection for A100 and RTX 6000, reducing p95 token latency by 18% for short-chat workloads.
- Added adaptive batch_wait_ms feature (auto-tuning mode) with conservative defaults.
- KV-cache admission policy updated to reduce cold-start I/O for long-context workloads.
- Fix: rare GPU OOM when switching heavy-quantized models with concurrent warm pool fill. Root cause: transient memory accounting race.

Release: runtime v3.7.1 (2026-01-07)
- Security: hardened RPC auth between routerd and inferd (mutual TLS & token expiry).
- Observability: per-kernel histograms added to profile-agent metrics.

6) Known issues and mitigations

K-101: Intermittent p99 spikes when mixing very short and very long requests on same GPU
- Symptoms: p50 stable, p99 jumps >2x during mixed workloads.
- Cause: batching head-of-line blocking due to large requests filling batch window.
- Mitigation: enable LATENCY_FIRST or separate workload classes to dedicated GPU pools. Use per-route isolation policy in routerd.

K-114: KV cache thrash after model swap
- Symptoms: high NVMe IOPS and increased cold-start latency for first 10 minutes after model swap.
- Mitigation: preload top-N prefixes during rollout (rollout hook: prewarm_prefixes.sh) and increase cache admission threshold during warm-up.

K-119: GPU memory accounting race (fixed in v3.8.0)
- Symptoms: occasional OOM during concurrent kernel pool fills.
- Mitigation: upgrade to v3.8.0; temporary workaround: set KERNEL_POOL_SIZE=1 on nodes running mixed quant models.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational procedures)

Oncall triage (first responder)
1. Confirm incident: check /status and alertgroup (pagerduty).
2. Gather quick metrics: p95/p99, GPU memory high-water marks, batch sizes, KV cache hit ratio.
3. If p99 spike: identify affected model variants and nodes via traces -> run node_profiler on affected nodes.
4. If OOM: drain node from routing, capture inferd logs, and run gdb heap-dump (see below).

GDB heap-dump (short procedure)
- sudo systemctl stop inferd --no-block
- sudo gdb --batch --pid $(pgrep inferd) -ex 'gcore /tmp/inferd.core' -ex detach
- scp /tmp/inferd.core to analysis host, then restart inferd.

Rolling upgrade procedure (minor runtime patch)
1. Create canary group (5% of traffic) and deploy runtime package.
2. Run bench/smoke small-chat against canary nodes for 10 minutes.
3. Monitor p50/p95/p99 and KV hit ratio.
4. If metrics stable, increment traffic by 20% every 10 minutes until 100%.
5. If regression detected, rollback via runtime-control rollback API.

Escalation matrix
- Level 1: Serving runtime oncall.
- Level 2: eng-sre for fleet/network issues.
- Level 3: Research/ML infra for kernel regression and model behavior.

Appendices

A: Common CLI & debug commands
- ./tools/replay_workload --trace <trace.json> --concurrency 16
- ./tools/node_profiler --target inferd://<node> --metrics kernel,mem --duration 120s
- curl -XPOST https://runtime-control.internal/v1/rollouts -d '{"model":"mymodel","percent":5}'

B: Config reference (important env vars)
- BATCH_WAIT_MS: wait window in ms for batching (string int). Default: "2".
- BATCH_MAX_TOKENS: max tokens per batch. Default: "65536".
- LATENCY_FIRST: boolean to favour low-latency small batches. Default: "true".
- KERNEL_POOL_SIZE: number of warmed kernels per model per GPU. Default: "2".
- GPU_RESERVED_MEM_MB: reserved memory for transient allocations. Default: "8192".
